A1.text:
There is a statue in a town. The statue is a prince. People call him the Happy Prince.

The statue is very tall. It stands high above the town. Gold covers the statue. Two blue sapphires are his eyes. A red ruby is on his sword.

One night, a swallow flies over the town. The swallow is tired. He wants to sleep. He sees the statue. He lands between the prince's feet.

"I have a golden bedroom," says the swallow. He starts to sleep. But a drop of water falls on him.

"That is strange," says the swallow. "The sky is clear. There are no clouds. But water falls on me."

Another drop falls. The swallow looks up. He sees the prince's face. The prince is crying.

"Why do you cry?" asks the swallow.

"When I was alive, I had a human heart," says the prince. "I lived in a palace. I did not know about sadness. Every day was happy. Now I am a statue. I can see all the sadness in my town. I can see poor people. I cry, but I cannot move. I cannot help them."

"There is a poor woman," says the prince. "She lives in a small house. Her son is sick. She has no money for food. Little swallow, will you take my ruby to her?"

The swallow does not want to stay. Winter is coming. His friends fly to Egypt. But the swallow feels sorry for the prince.

"I will stay one night," says the swallow. He takes the ruby. He flies to the poor house. He puts the ruby on the woman's table. The woman is very happy. Her son will have food now.

The next night, the prince speaks again. "Little swallow, will you stay one more night? I see a young man. He is a writer. He is cold and hungry. He cannot finish his play. Will you take one of my sapphire eyes to him?"

The swallow does not want to do this. "If I take your eye, you cannot see," he says. But he feels sorry for the prince. He takes the sapphire. He flies to the writer's room. He puts the sapphire on the table. The writer is very happy. He can buy food and wood for a fire.

The swallow wants to fly to Egypt. But the prince asks again. "Little swallow, I see a poor girl. She sells matches on the street. She has no shoes. If she does not sell her matches, her father will be angry. Will you take my other eye to her?"

"No! I cannot," says the swallow. "Then you will be blind."

"Please," says the prince.

The swallow feels very sad. But he takes the second sapphire. He flies to the girl. He puts the sapphire in her hand. The girl laughs and runs home.

Now the prince has no eyes. He cannot see the town. The swallow decides to stay with him. He tells the prince about the town every day. He tells him about rich people and poor people. He tells him about children who are hungry.

"Little swallow," says the prince. "My whole body is covered in gold. Take the gold, leaf by leaf. Give it to the poor people. People believe gold makes them happy."

The swallow takes the gold, piece by piece. He gives it to poor families. Soon the statue is not golden. It is grey.

Winter comes. Snow falls. The swallow is very cold. But he does not leave the prince. He loves him too much.

"Goodbye, dear prince," the swallow says one day. "I must kiss your hand."

"You must fly to Egypt now, little swallow," says the prince.

"No," says the swallow. "I will stay with you. I love you."

The swallow kisses the prince's lips. Then he falls down, dead, at the prince's feet.

At that moment, a strange sound comes from inside the statue. It is the sound of something breaking. The prince's leaden heart breaks in two.

The next morning, the Mayor and the Town Councillors walk by the statue.

"How shabby the Happy Prince looks!" says the Mayor. "The ruby is gone. The eyes are gone. He is not golden anymore. He is not beautiful."

"And there is a dead bird at his feet!" says another man. "We must make a new law. Birds must not die here."

The men take down the statue. They melt it in a fire. But the leaden heart does not melt. The workers throw it on a rubbish heap. They throw the dead swallow there too.

"Bring me the two most precious things in the town," God says to an angel.

The angel brings the leaden heart and the dead bird.

"You chose well," says God. "In my garden of Paradise, this little bird will sing forever. And in my city of gold, this Happy Prince will praise me forever."

A2.text:
High above the town stood a statue on a tall column. Everyone called it the Happy Prince, because its face always looked so cheerful. Thin gold leaves covered the whole statue, and its eyes were two bright sapphires. A red ruby shone on the handle of its sword.

Late one autumn night, a little swallow flew over the town. All his friends had already left for warm Egypt, but he had stayed behind because he had fallen in love with a beautiful reed by the river. When their romance ended, the swallow decided it was time to fly south too. As he traveled, tired and looking for a place to rest, he saw the statue and landed right between the prince's feet.

"I shall sleep in a golden bedroom tonight," he said happily, and got ready to sleep. But suddenly, a large drop of water fell on him.

"How curious!" thought the swallow. "There is not a single cloud in the sky, yet it is raining." Then another drop fell, and another. The swallow looked up and saw that the face of the Happy Prince was covered in tears.

"Why are you crying?" the swallow asked. "You have made me quite wet."

"When I was alive and had a human heart," the prince answered sadly, "I lived in a palace where sorrow was not allowed to enter. Every day I played in the garden with my friends, and every night I danced in the great hall. I never once thought about what lay outside the palace walls. Now that I am dead, they have put me up so high that I can see all the ugliness and misery of my city. Although my heart is made of lead, I cannot help but weep."

The prince told the swallow about a poor woman who lived in a small house across the town. Her little son was sick with fever, but she had no money to buy food or medicine. "Little swallow," the prince said, "will you carry the ruby from my sword to her? My feet are fixed to this pedestal, and I cannot move from this place."

The swallow did not really want to stay. Winter was coming, and it would soon be very cold. But he felt sorry for the prince, so he agreed to stay just one more night. He picked up the ruby in his beak and flew across the rooftops until he reached the poor woman's house. He left the jewel on the table beside her sewing, and the woman was overjoyed, for now she could buy food and medicine for her son.

The next night, the prince asked the swallow to stay again. This time he told him about a young writer who lived in a cold, bare room. The writer was trying to finish a play, but he was too hungry and cold to think clearly. "Will you take one of my sapphire eyes to him?" asked the prince.

"I cannot do that," said the swallow. "If I take your eye, you will be completely blind." But the prince begged him, so the swallow reluctantly agreed. He pulled out one of the beautiful sapphires and flew to the writer's attic room, leaving the jewel on his desk. The young man was amazed and delighted, and he was finally able to finish his play.

The swallow wanted to leave for Egypt at last, but the prince asked for one more favour. He told him about a poor little match-girl who had dropped all her matches in the gutter. If she went home without any money, her father would surely beat her. "Take my other eye to her," said the prince.

"No, I cannot!" cried the swallow. "Then you would be blind forever." Still, he could not refuse the sad prince. He took the last sapphire and flew down to the little girl, dropping the jewel into her hand. She laughed with delight and ran home.

Now the prince had no eyes at all, and he could no longer see his beloved city. The swallow, feeling great pity for him, decided he would stay with the prince forever and tell him stories about everything he saw. He described the rich people laughing in their fine houses, and the poor children shivering in doorways with nothing to eat.

"Little swallow," said the prince one day, "my whole body is covered with fine gold. Take it off, leaf by leaf, and give it to my poor people. Living people always believe that gold can make them happy."

Leaf by leaf, the swallow pulled off the fine gold, until the Happy Prince looked quite grey and dull. He carried each piece to poor families around the town, and everywhere he went, children's faces grew rosy and bright with joy.

Then the snow came, and after the snow came the frost. The little swallow grew colder and colder, but he would not leave the prince, for he loved him too much. He ate crumbs from the baker's doorway and flapped his wings to keep warm, but at last he knew that he was going to die.

He gathered just enough strength to fly up to the prince's shoulder. "Goodbye, dear prince," he whispered. "Will you let me kiss your hand?"

"I am glad that you are going to Egypt at last, little swallow," said the prince.

"I am not going to Egypt," said the swallow. "I am going to the House of Death. Death is the brother of Sleep, is he not?" And he kissed the prince on the lips, and fell down dead at his feet.

At that same moment, a strange cracking sound came from inside the statue, as if something had broken. In fact, the leaden heart of the prince had split cleanly in two, for it was a terribly hard frost that night.

Early the next morning, the Mayor was walking through the square with some Town Councillors. As they passed the column, the Mayor looked up.

"Dear me! How shabby the Happy Prince looks now!" he exclaimed. "The ruby has fallen from his sword, his eyes are gone, and he is no longer golden. In fact, he is hardly better than a beggar!"

"And here is a dead bird at his feet!" added one of the councillors. "We really must put up a notice that birds are not allowed to die here."

So the Town Councillors ordered that the statue be pulled down. It was melted in a furnace, but the broken leaden heart would not melt, no matter how hot the fire. The workers threw it onto a rubbish heap, where the dead swallow was also lying.

"Bring me the two most precious things in the city," God said to one of his angels. So the angel brought him the leaden heart and the dead bird.

"You have chosen rightly," said God, "for in my garden of Paradise this little bird shall sing for evermore, and in my city of gold the Happy Prince shall praise me."

B1.text:
High above the city, on top of a tall column, stood the statue of the Happy Prince. Thin sheets of gold covered his whole body, his eyes were two bright sapphires, and a red ruby shone on the handle of his sword.

Everybody admired him. One of the Town Councillors said the statue was as beautiful as a weathercock, although not quite as useful — he quickly added that, because he did not want people to think he was unpractical. A sensible mother told her crying son that he should be as content as the Happy Prince, who never cried for anything. A disappointed man, staring up at the statue, felt glad that at least someone in the world was truly happy. Even the children from the cathedral said the statue looked like an angel, though their teacher pointed out that none of them had ever actually seen one. "We have seen angels in our dreams," the children answered, which annoyed the teacher, because he did not approve of children dreaming.

One night, a little Swallow flew over the city. His friends had already left for Egypt weeks earlier, but he had stayed behind because he had fallen in love with a beautiful Reed by the river. In the end their romance did not work out — she cared only about her home, and he loved to travel — so he decided to fly south too. Tired from his journey, he landed to rest between the statue's feet.

"I have found a golden bedroom," he said happily, getting ready to sleep. But suddenly a large drop of water fell on him. Confused, since the sky was completely clear, he looked up — and saw that the Happy Prince's face was wet with tears.

"Why are you crying?" the Swallow asked.

"When I was alive, I had a human heart," the Prince explained. "I lived in a palace where sadness was never allowed to enter, and I never once wondered what lay beyond the palace walls. Now that I am dead, they have placed me up so high that I can see all the suffering of my city. My heart is made of lead, yet I cannot stop myself from weeping."

The Prince told the Swallow about a poor seamstress whose young son was sick with fever, with nothing but river water to drink. He asked the Swallow to carry the ruby from his sword to her house, since his own feet were fixed to the pedestal. The Swallow did not want to delay his trip to Egypt, but he felt sorry for the Prince, so he agreed to stay one more night. He flew across the rooftops and left the ruby on the woman's table; the boy soon felt cooler and began to recover.

The next night, the Prince asked the Swallow to stay again. This time he described a young writer, freezing in a bare room, unable to finish his play because hunger and cold made it impossible to think. The Prince asked the Swallow to take one of his sapphire eyes to him. The Swallow protested — "Then you will be blind!" — but the Prince insisted, so the Swallow carried the jewel to the writer's desk. Delighted, the young man was finally able to finish his play.

Although the Swallow wanted to continue his journey, the Prince made one last request. He pointed out a poor match-girl in the square below, who had dropped and ruined all her matches; if she went home with no money, her father would beat her. "Take my other eye to her," said the Prince. The Swallow refused at first, since this would leave the Prince completely blind, but he could not say no. He dropped the last sapphire into the girl's hand, and she ran home laughing.

Now that the Prince could no longer see his city, the Swallow decided to stay with him for good, describing everything he saw each day — the rich laughing in their fine houses, and the poor children shivering with nothing to eat. Moved by what he heard, the Prince asked the Swallow to strip off the fine gold that covered his body, leaf by leaf, and give it to the poor, since living people always believe that gold will make them happy. The Swallow carried away piece after piece, until the statue looked completely grey and plain, while all over the city poor children's faces grew brighter and happier.

Winter arrived, and the cold grew fierce. The Swallow, weak and freezing, refused to leave the Prince, whom he now loved too much to abandon. At last, sensing that he was about to die, he flew up to kiss the Prince's hand one final time.

"I am glad you are finally going to Egypt," said the Prince.

"I am not going to Egypt," the Swallow answered. "I am going to the House of Death." And he kissed the Prince on the lips, and fell down dead at his feet.

At that exact moment, a strange cracking sound came from inside the statue — the Prince's leaden heart had snapped cleanly in two.

The next morning, the Mayor and the Town Councillors walked past the column and were shocked at how shabby the once-glorious statue now looked: no ruby, no eyes, and no gold at all. "He is little better than a beggar," the Mayor declared, and — worse — there was a dead bird lying at his feet. The statue was pulled down at once and melted in a furnace. Strangely, the broken leaden heart would not melt, no matter how hot the fire burned, so the workers simply threw it onto a rubbish heap, right beside the body of the dead Swallow.

"Bring me the two most precious things in this city," God said to one of His angels. The angel brought Him the broken leaden heart and the dead bird.

"You have chosen well," said God. "In my garden of Paradise, this little bird shall sing forever, and in my city of gold, the Happy Prince shall praise me for all time."

B2.text:
High above the city, mounted on a tall column, stood the statue of the Happy Prince, gilded from head to foot in thin leaves of fine gold. His eyes were two bright sapphires, and a large red ruby glowed on the hilt of his sword. Everyone in the city admired him. A Town Councillor called him as beautiful as a weathercock, then quickly admitted he was not quite so useful, careful not to seem unpractical. A sensible mother scolded her crying son by asking why he could not be content, like the Happy Prince, who never wept for anything he wanted. Even the Charity Children, coming out of the cathedral in their scarlet cloaks, said the statue looked exactly like an angel — though their schoolmaster reminded them, rather sternly, that none of them had ever actually seen one. "We have," the children replied simply, "in our dreams."

One night a little Swallow flew over the city. He should have left for Egypt with the rest of his companions weeks before, but he had lingered behind, having fallen in love with a slender Reed on the riverbank. Their romance, however, went nowhere: she was too attached to her home to ever consider travelling with him, and eventually, feeling that she had only been trifling with his affections, he flew off in search of somewhere to spend the night. Seeing the tall statue, he decided it looked like a fine, airy spot, and settled himself between the Prince's feet.

"I shall sleep in a golden bedroom," he thought contentedly, tucking his head beneath his wing. But before he could fall asleep, a heavy drop of water landed on him, and then another. Puzzled, since the night sky held not a single cloud, he looked upward — and saw that the face of the Happy Prince was streaming with tears.

"Why are you weeping?" the Swallow asked. "You have quite drenched me."

"When I was alive, and had a human heart," the Prince answered, "I knew nothing of tears, for I lived in a palace where sorrow was never permitted to enter. I spent my days playing in the garden and my evenings dancing in the great hall, and I never once thought to ask what lay on the far side of the palace wall. Now that I am dead, they have raised me up so high that I can see all the ugliness and misery of my city, and though my heart is only lead, I cannot help but weep at what I see."

The Prince described a poor seamstress in a distant street, worn thin by work, whose small son lay ill with fever and could be given nothing but river water to drink. Since his own feet were fastened to the pedestal and he could not move, the Prince begged the Swallow to carry the ruby from his sword-hilt to her. Though he longed to continue on to Egypt, the Swallow was moved by the Prince's sorrow and agreed to stay one more night. He carried the jewel across the rooftops of the sleeping city and laid it gently on the woman's table; almost at once, her fevered child grew calm and fell into a peaceful sleep.

The following night, the Prince made a second request. Across the city, in a bare and freezing garret, a young playwright sat struggling to finish a play, too cold and hungry to think clearly. "Will you take him one of my sapphire eyes?" the Prince asked. The Swallow was horrified — "Then you will be quite blind" — but could not refuse, and so plucked out one brilliant sapphire and carried it to the young man's desk. Astonished by the gem lying among his withered flowers, the writer took new heart, and soon the play was finished.

Eager at last to leave for warmer skies, the Swallow was stopped by one final plea. In the square below, the Prince had noticed a poor match-girl who had let her matches fall into the gutter, ruining them all; if she returned home without any money, her father would surely beat her. "Pluck out my other eye," said the Prince, "and give it to her." Though it meant leaving the Prince entirely blind, the Swallow could not bear to refuse, and dropped the last sapphire into the girl's open palm. She laughed with delight, certain she had found nothing more than a pretty piece of glass, and ran home.

With the Prince now sightless, the Swallow resolved to remain with him always, and each day he flew over the city and returned to describe everything he had seen — the rich feasting behind lit windows, and the poor huddled hungry in the streets below. Moved beyond words by these stories, the Prince asked the Swallow to strip the fine gold from his body, leaf by leaf, and carry it to the poor, for the living, he said, always believe that gold can make them happy. Leaf by leaf the gold came away, until the once-glittering statue stood dull and grey, while throughout the city hungry children grew rosy-cheeked and laughed once more in the streets.

Then came the snow, and after the snow, a bitter frost. The Swallow, half-frozen, refused to abandon the Prince, for by now he loved him too dearly to leave. At last, feeling his strength fail entirely, he gathered himself for one final flight to the Prince's shoulder. "Farewell, dear Prince," he murmured. "Will you let me kiss your hand?"

"I am glad you are finally leaving for Egypt, little Swallow," said the Prince.

"It is not Egypt I am going to," the Swallow answered. "I am going to the House of Death." And kissing the Prince once upon the lips, he fell down dead at his feet.

At that very instant, a strange sound cracked from somewhere deep inside the statue — as though something inside it had broken clean in two. It was, in fact, the Prince's leaden heart, split apart by the terrible cold of that night.

Early the next morning, as the Mayor walked through the square with his Town Councillors, he glanced up at the column and stopped short. "How shabby the Happy Prince looks now!" he exclaimed — the ruby gone from his sword, his eyes vanished, his gold stripped bare, until he appeared little better than a common beggar. And worse, a dead bird lay at his feet. The statue was pulled down without delay and melted in a furnace, yet the broken leaden heart refused to melt no matter how fierce the flames grew, so the workmen simply cast it onto a heap of rubbish, alongside the body of the dead Swallow.

"Bring me the two most precious things in this city," God said to one of His angels, and the angel returned bearing the broken leaden heart and the small dead bird.

"You have chosen rightly," said God, "for in my garden of Paradise this little bird shall sing forevermore, and in my city of gold the Happy Prince shall praise me for all eternity."
